title: the coronation planned
hook: a whole city stays up all night getting ready for one morning

segments.voice: Yesterday: the coronation planned, and rushed to the next morning, while Bharata was away. Did you slow down one good thing and ask who it left out? Today, the city gets ready. Day five hundred sixteen.

If you've ever been in a town the night before a big festival, you know the sound. Ladders against walls. Someone sweeping a street that was already swept. Lights going up in trees. Children who should be asleep, absolutely not asleep. Valmiki gives us Ayodhya on that night, and he takes his time with it. He wants you to see how happy the city is, so you'll feel what it loses by morning.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE A FESTIVAL.` → `LIGHTS IN THE TREES.` → `SO YOU'LL FEEL THE LOSS.`

segments.voice: Start with Rama. Before the night's fast, he goes to his mother Kausalya's rooms, and Lakshmana is there. Rama turns to him and says, in effect: this is yours too. Rule the earth with me. You are my second self. It's a small line, and it tells you who these brothers are to each other. Then the city. Word has spread, and the people of Ayodhya can't keep still. Streets are sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers. Banners go up on the houses. Lamps are hung on trees along the roads so that night looks like day. People gather in the squares and talk about nothing else. The old king is going to make Rama heir, they say to each other. What good fortune for us. Meanwhile Vasishtha's helpers gather what the rite will need. The word for the rite is abhisheka, an anointing, a pouring. The heir is bathed with sacred waters, and the text lists the things made ready: gold, white flowers, parched grain, honey and ghee, a white umbrella of state, yak-tail fans, a decorated elephant, waters from holy rivers. All of this is for a pouring that will happen at dawn. And all of it, in a few hours, will sit unused. The beauty of today's passage is that nobody in it is doing anything wrong. A father loves his son. A brother is invited to share. A city celebrates. Valmiki gives this happiness its full weight, so that when it breaks, nothing about it feels small. One person, though, has gone up on a rooftop, and she's looking down at all the lights.
screen: `YOU ARE MY SECOND SELF.` · `A CITY THAT CAN'T KEEP STILL.` · `ABHISHEKA: A POURING AT DAWN.` · `HAPPINESS GIVEN FULL WEIGHT.` · then, large: `SOMEONE ON A ROOFTOP.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture Ayodhya that night: the swept streets, the flowers, the lamps in the trees. Now bring to mind something good in your own life right now, a person, a season, a small routine you love. Let yourself enjoy it fully for these two minutes, without guarding it, without thinking about how long it lasts. Just let it be as bright as it is. The bell holds the time.
The coronation planned, and prepared. Ayodhya decorates itself overnight, and everything for the abhisheka, the anointing, is made ready for dawn.
Your line: the coronation planned. Today, tell someone you share a good thing with that it's theirs too. Day five hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Abhisheka, the ritual bathing or pouring, is still central to Hindu worship: temple images are bathed with water, milk and other offerings, and royal consecrations once followed the same pattern.

original.note: Sanskrit abhiṣeka: a sprinkling or pouring over. the rite of consecration, and still the word for bathing a temple image.

trapdoor: what you thought: a coronation means putting on a crown.
what it means: the heart of the rite is abhisheka, pouring sacred waters over the heir.
what a scholar hears: the consecration of kings in Vedic ritual texts is also built around an anointing with waters, and the epic's list of materials echoes that older pattern.
